items.stem: A music service compresses each song's 500 audio features into 10 features that capture most of the variation. Which type of machine learning is this?
options: supervised learning
unsupervised learning
semi-supervised learning
reinforcement learning
items.answer: unsupervised learning
items.markingKey: B. unsupervised learning: no labels; it finds a lower-dimensional representation.

items.stem: "A machine-learning model follows rules written by its programmer." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: The programmer writes the learning algorithm; the decision rules (parameters) are learned from data.
items.markingKey: The programmer writes the learning algorithm; the decision rules (parameters) are learned from data. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why reinforcement learning suits game playing and robotics.
items.answer: There is often no labelled "correct move" for every situation, but outcomes (win/lose, task completed) give a reward signal; the agent can learn a strategy through repeated trial and error. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: There is often no labelled "correct move" for every situation, but outcomes (win/lose, task completed) give a reward signal; the agent can learn a strategy through repeated trial and error. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: An online shop finds that customers who buy tents often also buy head torches. State which type of machine learning this is and explain how you can tell.
items.answer: unsupervised learning (association rule learning) – rules are mined from unlabelled transaction data
items.markingKey: unsupervised learning (association rule learning) (1); justification: rules are mined from unlabelled transaction data (1).

items.stem:
(a) State what is meant by the term "feature". [2]
(b) A student claims that a machine-learning model follows rules written by its programmer. Identify the error in this claim and correct it. [2]
(c) A climate lab labels a few hundred satellite images as "flooded" and uses them together with a million unlabelled images to train a classifier. Classify this application as supervised, unsupervised, semi-supervised or reinforcement learning, giving a reason. [2]
items.answer: (a) A measurable input property of the data used by a model, such as age or pixel brightness (b) The programmer writes the learning algorithm; the decision rules (parameters) are learned from data. (c) semi-supervised learning – a small labelled set is combined with a large unlabelled set
items.markingKey: (a) [2 marks] 1 mark for the core idea: a measurable input property of the data used by a model, such as age or pixel brightness. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0. (c) [2 marks] semi-supervised learning (1); justification: a small labelled set is combined with a large unlabelled set (1).

items.stem:
Case study context: MetroFlow, the public-transport authority in Kuala Lumpur, stores ticketing data in a data warehouse, predicts passenger demand with machine learning and runs route-planning software built from classes and graph structures.
(a) Distinguish between reinforcement learning and supervised learning. Refer to MetroFlow in your answer. [3]
(b) Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Supervised learning is always more accurate than unsupervised learning." Refer to MetroFlow in your answer. [3]
items.answer: (a) Supervised learning is told the correct output for each example; reinforcement learning only receives a reward signal after actions and must discover good actions by exploration. (b) The comparison is misplaced: the choice depends on the task and on whether reliable labels exist.
items.markingKey: (a) [3 marks] Supervised learning is told the correct output for each example; reinforcement learning only receives a reward signal after actions and must discover good actions by exploration. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions). (b) [3 marks] Arguments for: labels give a clear objective and measurable accuracy; well-suited to prediction tasks. Arguments against: the two solve different problems so accuracy is not directly comparable; supervised models are limited by label quality and quantity; unsupervised learning can reveal unknown patterns. Supported judgement: The comparison is misplaced: the choice depends on the task and on whether reliable labels exist. Credit is given only for points applied to the stated organisation (not generic answers).

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "semi-supervised learning"?
options: Learning from a small amount of labelled data together with a large amount of unlabelled data
A model made of layers of connected artificial neurons, each computing a weighted sum of its inputs plus a bias passed through an activation function
The examples used to fit a model's parameters
Renting remote, scalable compute and storage (e.g. GPU clusters) over the internet to train or serve models
items.answer: Learning from a small amount of labelled data together with a large amount of unlabelled data
items.markingKey: A. "semi-supervised learning" is learning from a small amount of labelled data together with a large amount of unlabelled data.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "label".
items.answer: The known correct output (target) attached to a training example in supervised learning
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the known correct output (target) attached to a training example in supervised learning. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain the difference between unsupervised learning and supervised learning.
items.answer: Supervised learning trains on labelled data to predict known outputs; unsupervised learning finds structure in unlabelled data without target outputs.
items.markingKey: Supervised learning trains on labelled data to predict known outputs; unsupervised learning finds structure in unlabelled data without target outputs. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Assertion (A): k-means clustering is a supervised learning algorithm.
Reason (R): k-means needs the number of clusters k to be chosen.
Which option is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
items.answer: A is false but R is true.
items.markingKey: D. A is false (unsupervised); R is true.

items.stem: Distinguish between unsupervised learning and supervised learning.

items.stem: Amara writes: "Reinforcement learning is supervised learning with rewards as labels." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Rewards are delayed and evaluate sequences of actions, not correct answers for each input; the agent must balance exploration and exploitation.
items.markingKey: Rewards are delayed and evaluate sequences of actions, not correct answers for each input; the agent must balance exploration and exploitation. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: An estate agency in Lisbon predicts the selling price of flats from their size, location and age using past sales. Classify this application as supervised, unsupervised, semi-supervised or reinforcement learning, giving a reason.
items.answer: supervised learning (regression) – labelled examples with a continuous numerical target (price)
items.markingKey: supervised learning (regression) (1); justification: labelled examples with a continuous numerical target (price) (1).

items.stem:
Compare the machine-learning approaches needed for these two applications, referring to the data each requires and how each model is trained.
Application 1: An email provider learns to sort messages into "spam" and "not spam" from messages users have marked.
Application 2: A supermarket in Hanoi groups its loyalty-card customers into segments based on what they buy, without any predefined groups.
items.answer: 1: supervised learning (classification) – the user-marked messages provide labels. 2: unsupervised learning (clustering) – there are no labels; the algorithm discovers structure (groups) in the data.
items.markingKey: Application 1 is supervised learning (classification) because the user-marked messages provide labels (2). Application 2 is unsupervised learning (clustering) because there are no labels; the algorithm discovers structure (groups) in the data (2). Comparison of data needed (labelled/unlabelled/reward signal) and training process (fit to labels / discover structure / trial-and-error with rewards) (2).

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A graphics processing unit: a processor with thousands of simple cores that perform the same operation on many data items in parallel, ideal for the matrix operations in ML"?
options: cloud computing (for ML)
machine learning
FPGA
GPU
items.answer: GPU
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of GPU.

items.stem: A student claims that any ML model can run on a smartwatch if the code is efficient. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Large models need more memory and compute than a watch has; they must be compressed (quantised, pruned, distilled) or run in the cloud.
items.markingKey: Large models need more memory and compute than a watch has; they must be compressed (quantised, pruned, distilled) or run in the cloud. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between edge ML and cloud ML.
items.answer: Cloud ML runs on remote, powerful servers (scalable, needs connectivity); edge ML runs on local devices (low latency, private, limited resources).

items.stem: Why are GPUs preferred to CPUs for training neural networks?
options: They use less memory
They have higher clock speeds
They can only run Python
They perform many matrix multiplications in parallel
items.answer: They perform many matrix multiplications in parallel
items.markingKey: D. Massive parallelism suits matrix maths.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "edge computing"?
options: Running processing, such as ML inference, on or near the device where data is produced rather than in a distant data centre
The examples used to fit a model's parameters
Learning patterns or structure, such as clusters or associations, from data that has no labels
Renting remote, scalable compute and storage (e.g. GPU clusters) over the internet to train or serve models

items.stem: Explain why many ML applications run inference on edge devices rather than in the cloud.
items.answer: Lower latency (no network round trip), works offline, keeps personal data on the device (privacy), and reduces bandwidth and server cost; the trade-off is limited device memory and power.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Lower latency (no network round trip), works offline, keeps personal data on the device (privacy), and reduces bandwidth and server cost; the trade-off is limited device memory and power. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between training and inference.
items.answer: Training fits the model's parameters using large datasets and is compute-intensive; inference applies the trained model to new inputs and is relatively cheap.
items.markingKey: Training fits the model's parameters using large datasets and is compute-intensive; inference applies the trained model to new inputs and is relatively cheap. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Omar writes: "Machine learning is only used by technology companies." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: It is used in healthcare (diagnosis), agriculture (yield prediction), finance (fraud detection), transport (demand forecasting), retail (recommendations) and many other sectors.

items.answer: A shallow network has one (or very few) hidden layers; a deep network has many, allowing it to build hierarchical representations.

items.stem:

(a) Explain the difference between machine learning and deep learning. Refer to Saigon Fresh in your answer. [3]
(b) Analyse one strength and one limitation of the view that Deep learning is the best approach for every machine-learning problem. Refer to Saigon Fresh in your answer. [3]
items.answer: (a) Classical ML often relies on hand-engineered features and simpler models; deep learning uses many-layered neural networks that learn features automatically from raw data, needing more data and compute. (b) No: deep learning excels on large unstructured data; for small or tabular datasets and where explanations are required, simpler models are often better.

items.stem: A rule-based expert system for diagnosing faults in a car is an example of…

unsupervised learning
AI that is not machine learning
deep learning
items.answer: AI that is not machine learning

items.stem: Explain why deep learning needs large datasets.
items.answer: Deep networks have very many parameters; with little data they memorise the training set (overfit) instead of learning general features, so many examples are needed to constrain the parameters.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Deep networks have very many parameters; with little data they memorise the training set (overfit) instead of learning general features, so many examples are needed to constrain the parameters. items.stem:
Compare the machine-learning approaches needed for these two applications, referring to the data each requires and how each model is trained.
Application 1: A supermarket in Hanoi groups its loyalty-card customers into segments based on what they buy, without any predefined groups.
Application 2: A credit-card company flags transactions that are very unlike a customer's usual spending, without labelled fraud examples.
items.answer: 1: unsupervised learning (clustering) – there are no labels; the algorithm discovers structure (groups) in the data. 2: unsupervised learning (anomaly detection) – it learns normal patterns from unlabelled data and flags outliers.
items.markingKey: Application 1 is unsupervised learning (clustering) because there are no labels; the algorithm discovers structure (groups) in the data (2). Application 2 is unsupervised learning (anomaly detection) because it learns normal patterns from unlabelled data and flags outliers (2). Comparison of data needed (labelled/unlabelled/reward signal) and training process (fit to labels / discover structure / trial-and-error with rewards) (2).

items.stem:
Case study context: Kente Market, an online craft marketplace in Accra, stores products as JSON documents, ranks listings with a neural network and processes orders through a queue-based service.
(a) With the help of a specific example, explain why training a large model needs far more computing power than using it. Refer to Kente Market in your answer. [2]
(b) "Specialised hardware such as TPUs will make general-purpose GPUs obsolete for machine learning." To what extent do you agree with this statement? Refer to Kente Market in your answer. [4]
items.answer: (a) Training repeats forward and backward passes over the whole dataset many times (epochs) to adjust millions or billions of parameters, while inference is a single forward pass per input. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (b) Specialised chips will take an increasing share of large-scale workloads, but GPUs remain important because of flexibility and ecosystem support.
items.markingKey: (a) [2 marks] Award marks for: Training repeats forward and backward passes over the whole dataset many times (epochs) to adjust millions or billions of parameters, while inference is a single forward pass per input. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.) (b) [4 marks] Arguments for: TPUs give higher performance per watt for tensor operations; large providers deploy them at scale. Arguments against: GPUs are flexible, widely available and supported by all ML frameworks; new model types may not suit fixed-function chips; cost and vendor lock-in. Supported judgement: Specialised chips will take an increasing share of large-scale workloads, but GPUs remain important because of flexibility and ecosystem support.
